{{Short description|Set of problems solved by small circuits}}
In [[computational complexity theory]], '''P/poly''' is a [[complexity class]] that can be defined in both [[circuit complexity]] and [[Circuit complexity#Uniformity|non-uniform complexity]]. Since the two definitions are equivalent, this concept bridges the two areas.

In the perspective of circuit complexity, '''P/poly''' is the class of problems that can be solved by small circuits. More precisely, it is the set of [[formal language]]s that have polynomial-size circuit families. 

In the perspective of non-uniform complexity, '''P/poly''' is defined in terms of [[Turing machine]]s with [[advice (complexity)|advice]], extra information supplied to the Turing machine along with its input, that may depend on the input length but not on the input itself. In this formulation, '''P/poly''' is the class of [[decision problem]]s that can be solved by a polynomial-time [[Turing machine]] with advice strings of length polynomial in the input size.<ref name="lutz93" /><ref>{{citation |url=http://www.daimi.au.dk/~bromille/CT06/complex3.pdf |title=Lecture notes on computational complexity by Peter Bro Miltersen |access-date=2009-12-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120223150858/http://www.daimi.au.dk/~bromille/CT06/complex3.pdf |archive-date=2012-02-23 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

For example, the popular [[Miller–Rabin primality test]] can be formulated as a '''P/poly''' algorithm: the "advice" is a list of candidate values to test. It is possible to precompute a list of <math>O(n)</math> values such that every composite {{mvar|n}}-bit number will be certain to have a witness {{mvar|a}} in the list.<ref name="gw02">{{citation
 | last1 = Goldreich | first1 = Oded | author1-link = Oded Goldreich
 | last2 = Wigderson | first2 = Avi | author2-link = Avi Wigderson
 | editor1-last = Rolim | editor1-first = José D. P.
 | editor2-last = Vadhan | editor2-first = Salil P.
 | contribution = Derandomization that is rarely wrong from short advice that is typically good
 | doi = 10.1007/3-540-45726-7_17
 | id = {{ECCC|2002|02|39}}
 | pages = 209–223
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Randomization and Approximation Techniques, 6th International Workshop, RANDOM 2002, Cambridge, MA, USA, September 13-15, 2002, Proceedings
 | volume = 2483
 | year = 2002}}</ref> For example, to correctly determine the primality of 32-bit numbers, it is enough to test <math>a\in\{2,7,61\}</math>.<ref>{{citation|first=Chris|last=Caldwell|url=http://primes.utm.edu/prove/prove2_3.html|title=2.3: Strong probable-primality and a practical test|work=Finding primes & proving primality}}</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Jaeschke | first = Gerhard
 | doi = 10.2307/2153262
 | issue = 204
 | journal = Mathematics of Computation
 | mr = 1192971
 | pages = 915–926
 | title = On strong pseudoprimes to several bases
 | volume = 61
 | year = 1993| doi-access = free
 }}; see p. 926.</ref> The existence of short lists of candidate witnesses follows from the fact that for each composite {{mvar|n}}, three out of four candidate values successfully detect that {{mvar|n}} is composite. From this, a simple counting argument similar to the one in the proof that <math>\mathsf{BPP} \subset \mathsf{P/poly}</math> below shows that there exists a suitable list of candidate values for every input size, and more strongly that most long-enough lists of candidate values will work correctly, although finding a list that is guaranteed to work may be expensive.<ref name="gw02" />

'''P/poly''', unlike other polynomial-time classes such as '''[[P (complexity)|P]]''' or '''[[Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial|BPP]]''', is not generally considered a practical class for computing. Indeed, it contains every [[undecidable problem|undecidable]] [[unary language]], none of which can be solved in general by real computers. On the other hand, if the input length is bounded by a relatively small number and the advice strings are short, it can be used to model practical algorithms with a separate expensive preprocessing phase and a fast processing phase, as in the Miller–Rabin example.

== Formal definition ==
The [[complexity class]] '''P/poly''' can be defined in terms of '''SIZE''' as follows:

:<math>\mathsf{P/poly} = \bigcup_{c\in\mathbb{N}} \mathsf{SIZE}(n^c),</math>

where <math>\mathsf{SIZE}(n^c)</math> is the set of [[decision problem|decision problems]] that can be solved by circuit families having no more than <math>n^c</math> gates on inputs of size <math>n</math>.

Alternatively, <math>\mathsf{P/poly}</math> can be defined using [[Turing machine|Turing machines]] that "take advice". Such a machine has, for each {{mvar|n}}, an ''[[advice (complexity)|advice string]]'' <math>\alpha_n</math>, which it is allowed to use in its computation whenever the input has size {{mvar|n}}. To help visualize this equivalence, imagine that the advice for each {{mvar|n}} is a description of a Boolean circuit having {{mvar|n}} inputs, and that a Turing Machine for the language merely evaluates the given Boolean circuit on inputs of length {{mvar|n}}.

Let <math>T,a: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}</math> be functions. The class of languages decidable by time-T(n) [[Turing machine|Turing machines]] with <math>a(n)</math> advice, denoted <math>\mathsf{DTIME}(T(n))/a(n)</math>, contains every language ''L'' such that there exists a sequence <math>\{\alpha_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}</math> of strings with <math>\alpha_n \in \{0, 1\}^{a(n)}</math> and a TM ''M'' satisfying

:<math>M(x, \alpha_n) = 1 \Leftrightarrow x \in L</math>

for every <math>x \in \{0, 1\}^n</math>, where on input <math>(x, \alpha_n)</math> the machine ''M'' runs for at most <math>O(T(n))</math> steps.<ref>{{citation | zbl=1193.68112 | last1=Arora | first1=Sanjeev | authorlink1=Sanjeev Arora (computer scientist) | last2=Barak | first2=Boaz | title=Computational complexity. A modern approach | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year=2009 | isbn=978-0-521-42426-4 }}</ref>

== Importance of P/poly ==
'''P/poly''' is an important class for several reasons.  For theoretical computer science, there are several important properties that depend on '''P/poly''':

* If '''[[NP (complexity)|NP]]''' ⊆ '''P/poly''' then '''PH''' (the [[polynomial hierarchy]]) collapses to <math>\Sigma_2^{\mathsf P}</math>. This result is the [[Karp–Lipton theorem]]; furthermore,  '''NP''' ⊆ '''P/poly''' implies '''[[Arthur–Merlin protocol|AM]]''' = '''MA''' <ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Arvind | first1 = Vikraman
 | last2 = Köbler | first2 = Johannes
 | last3 = Schöning | first3 = Uwe | author3-link = Uwe Schöning
 | last4 = Schuler | first4 = Rainer
 | doi = 10.1016/0304-3975(95)91133-B
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Theoretical Computer Science (journal)|Theoretical Computer Science]]
 | mr = 1311226
 | pages = 279–282
 | title = If NP has polynomial-size circuits, then MA = AM
 | url = http://www.informatik.hu-berlin.de/forschung/gebiete/algorithmenII/Publikationen/Papers/ma-am.ps.gz
 | volume = 137
 | year = 1995| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>
* If '''[[PSPACE]]''' ⊆ '''P/poly''' then <math>\mathsf{PSPACE} = \Sigma_2^{\mathsf P} \cap \Pi_2^{\mathsf P}</math>, even '''PSPACE''' = '''MA'''.
:Proof: Consider a language ''L'' from '''PSPACE'''. It is known that there exists an [[IP (complexity)|interactive proof system]] for ''L'', where actions of the prover can be carried out by a '''PSPACE''' machine. By assumption, the prover can be replaced by a polynomial-size circuit. Therefore, ''L'' has a '''MA''' protocol: Merlin sends the circuit as proof, and Arthur can simulate the '''IP''' protocol himself without any additional help.
* If '''P<sup>[[Sharp P|#P]]</sup>''' ⊆ '''P/poly''' then '''P<sup>#P</sup>''' = '''MA'''.<ref>{{citation

 | first1 = László

 | author3-link = Carsten Lund
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01200056
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Computational Complexity
 | mr = 1113533
 | pages = 3–40
 | title = Nondeterministic exponential time has two-prover interactive protocols
 | url = http://www.cs.uchicago.edu/files/tr_authentic/TR-91-10.ps
 | volume = 1
 | year = 1991
 | access-date = 2011-10-02
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120331215832/http://www.cs.uchicago.edu/files/tr_authentic/TR-91-10.ps
 | archive-date = 2012-03-31
 | url-status = dead
 }}</ref>  The proof is similar to above, based on an interactive protocol for permanent and [[Permanent is sharp-P-complete|#P-completeness of permanent]].
* If '''[[EXPTIME]]''' ⊆ '''P/poly''' then <math>\mathsf{EXPTIME} =\Sigma_2^{\mathsf P} \cap \Pi_2^{\mathsf P}</math> (Meyer's theorem), even '''EXPTIME''' = '''MA'''.
* If '''[[NEXPTIME]]''' ⊆ '''P/poly''' then '''NEXPTIME''' = '''EXPTIME''', even '''NEXPTIME''' = '''MA'''. Conversely, '''NEXPTIME''' = '''MA''' implies '''NEXPTIME''' ⊆ '''P/poly'''<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Impagliazzo | first1 = Russell | author1-link = Russell Impagliazzo
 | last2 = Kabanets | first2 = Valentine
 | last3 = Wigderson | first3 = Avi | author3-link = Avi Wigderson
 | doi = 10.1016/S0022-0000(02)00024-7

 | url = http://www.math.ias.edu/~avi/PUBLICATIONS/MYPAPERS/IKW02/IKW02.pdf

 | year = 2002}}</ref>
* If '''EXP'''<sup>'''NP'''</sup> ⊆ '''P/poly''' then <math>\mathsf{EXP^{NP}} = \Sigma_2^{\mathsf P} \cap \Pi_2^{\mathsf P}</math> (Buhrman, Homer) <ref>[http://cse.unl.edu/~cbourke/pubs/EXPnote.pdf A Note on the Karp-Lipton Collapse for the Exponential Hierarchy]</ref>
* It is known that '''MA'''<sub>EXP</sub>, an exponential version of '''[[Arthur–Merlin protocol|MA]]''', is not contained in '''P/poly'''.
: Proof: If '''MA'''<sub>EXP</sub> ⊆ '''P/poly''' then '''PSPACE''' = '''MA''' (see above). By [[padding argument|padding]], '''EXPSPACE''' = '''MA'''<sub>EXP</sub>, therefore '''EXPSPACE''' ⊆ '''P/poly''' but this can be proven false with diagonalization.
*The best known bound for the [[square-root sum problem]] is in the fourth level of the counting hierarchy, and it is an unsolved problem whether better complexity is possible, but a unary version of the problem is in '''P/poly'''.<ref>{{citation

One of the most interesting reasons that '''P/poly''' is important is the property that if '''NP''' is not a subset of '''P/poly''', then '''P''' ≠ '''NP'''.  This observation was the center of many attempts to prove '''P''' ≠ '''NP'''. It is known that for a random oracle ''A'', '''NP'''<sup>''A''</sup> is not a subset of '''P'''<sup>A</sup>'''/poly''' with probability 1.<ref name="lutz93">{{citation
 | last = Lutz | first = Jack H.
 | last2 = Schmidt | first2 = William J.
 | doi = 10.1016/0304-3975(93)90256-S
 | issue = 1
 | mr = 1201167
 | title = Circuit size relative to pseudorandom oracles
 | pages = 95–119
 | journal = [[Theoretical Computer Science (journal)|Theoretical Computer Science]]
 | volume = 107
 | year = 1993| doi-access = 
 }}</ref>

'''P/poly''' is also used in the field of [[cryptography]].  Security is often defined 'against' '''P/poly''' adversaries. Besides including most practical models of computation like '''BPP''', this also admits the possibility that adversaries can do heavy precomputation for inputs up to a certain length, as in the construction of [[rainbow table]]s.

Although not all languages in '''P/poly''' are [[sparse language]]s, there is a [[polynomial-time Turing reduction]] from any language in '''P/poly''' to a sparse language.<ref>Jin-Yi Cai. [http://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~jyc/02-810notes/lecture11.pdf Lecture 11: P/poly, Sparse Sets, and Mahaney's Theorem]. CS 810: Introduction to Complexity Theory. The University of Wisconsin–Madison. September 18, 2003.</ref>

== Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial is contained in P/poly ==
Adleman's theorem states that '''[[Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial|BPP]]''' ⊆ '''P/poly''', where '''BPP''' is the set of problems solvable with randomized algorithms with two-sided error in polynomial time. A weaker result was initially proven by [[Leonard Adleman]], namely, that '''[[RP (complexity)|RP]]''' ⊆ '''P/poly''';<ref>{{citation
 | last = Adleman | first = L. M. | author-link = Leonard Adleman
 | contribution = Two theorems on random polynomial time
 | doi = 10.1109/SFCS.1978.37
 | pages = 75–83
 | title = Proceedings of the Nineteenth Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science
 | year = 1978| title-link = Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science }}</ref> and this result was generalized to '''BPP''' ⊆ '''P/poly''' by [[Charles H. Bennett (computer scientist)|Bennett]] and Gill.<ref>Charles H. Bennett, John Gill. ''Relative to a Random Oracle A, P<sup>A</sup> ≠ NP<sup>A</sup> ≠ co-NP<sup>A</sup> with probability 1''. [https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs682/2006sp/handouts/bennettgill.pdf]{{Open access}}</ref>
Variants of the theorem show that '''[[BPL (complexity)|BPL]]''' is contained in '''[[L/poly]]''' and '''AM''' is contained in '''[[NP/poly]]'''.

=== Proof ===
Let ''L'' be a language in '''BPP''', and let ''M''(''x'',''r'') be a polynomial-time algorithm that decides ''L'' with error ≤ 1/3 (where ''x'' is the input string and ''r'' is a set of random bits).

Construct a new machine ''{{prime|M}}''(''x'',''R''), which runs ''M'' 48''n'' times and takes a majority vote of the results (where ''n'' is the input length and ''R'' is a sequence of 48''n'' independently random ''r''s).  Thus, ''{{prime|M}}'' is also polynomial-time, and has an error probability ≤ 1/''e''<sup>''n''</sup> by the [[Chernoff bound]] (see [[Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial|BPP]]). If we can fix ''R'' then we obtain an algorithm that is deterministic.

If <math>\mbox{Bad}(x)</math> is defined as <math>\{R: M{{'}}(x, R) \text{ is incorrect}\}</math>, we have:

:<math>\forall x\, \mbox{Prob}_R[R \in \mbox{Bad}(x)] \leq \frac{1}{e^n}.</math>

The input size is ''n'', so there are 2<sup>''n''</sup> possible inputs. Thus, by the [[union bound]], the probability that a random ''R'' is bad for at least one input ''x'' is

:<math>\mbox{Prob}_R [\exists x\,R \in \mbox{Bad}(x)] \leq \frac{2^n}{e^n} < 1.</math>

In words, the probability that ''R'' is bad for at least one ''x'' is less than 1, therefore there must be an ''R'' that is good for all ''x''. Take such an ''R'' to be the advice string in our '''P/poly''' algorithm.
